questions.stem: State the standard enthalpy change of formation definition in full.
questions.modelAnswer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions of 100 kPa and 298 K.

questions.stem: List the five standard enthalpy changes by name.
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation and atomisation.

questions.stem: Explain why states of matter must be specified in these definitions.
questions.modelAnswer: Enthalpy depends on the physical state - gas, liquid or solid hold different energy contents - so an unstated state leaves the defined quantity ambiguous.

questions.stem: Write the standard formation equation for ammonia, NH3(g), and state the standard conditions that apply to it.
questions.modelAnswer: (1/2)N2(g) + (3/2)H2(g) -> NH3(g), quoted at 100 kPa and 298 K with every species gaseous in its standard state.

questions.stem: State why an element's standard formation enthalpy is zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Elements in their standard states are the reference floor from which all formation enthalpies are measured, so their own formation change is zero by definition.

questions.stem: Write the formation equation for methanol, CH3OH(l), from its elements.
questions.modelAnswer: C(s) + 2H2(g) + (1/2)O2(g) -> CH3OH(l), with every element in its standard state and one mole of product.

questions.stem: Explain why the one-mole product rule matters when writing formation equations.
questions.modelAnswer: Formation enthalpies feed Hess cycles as per-mole quantities, so an equation making two moles would deliver the wrong scale into every cycle built on it - the rule keeps the table additive.

questions.stem: Write the standard formation equation for propan-1-ol, C3H7OH(l), and verify the hydrogen count.
questions.modelAnswer: 3C(s) + 4H2(g) + (1/2)O2(g) -> C3H7OH(l): the elements' hydrogens total 4 x 2 = 8, matching the product's 7 + 1 = 8 hydrogens.
